prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and interest-rate policy rules, and for integrating them into the welfare-based framework used to analyse monetary policy

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part B014 prize to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. I tightened the citation after the chair's question. It is now confined to nominal-rigidity theory, staggered contracts, policy rules and the welfare-based synthesis. It does not claim to honour the estimated medium-scale DSGE strand or the empirical performance of the baseline Phillips curve. The case rests on three separable, traceable contributions. Calvo supplied the time-dependent pricing device that most New Keynesian models use. Taylor supplied staggered contracts and an interest-rate rule that became a common language for policy analysis. Woodford supplied the microfounded, welfare-based synthesis that turned these pieces into a framework for evaluating policy. The work is 25 to 40 years old, so it has been extended, criticised and used in institutions for a long time. I treat this as a judgement about originality, durability and consequence, not a count of supporters. I know the round 1 exchange shows no position near six, and I do not read that as a reason to dilute attribution into a compromise. I would rather be explicit about which strand is honoured and defend that choice on stated criteria.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the main weakness. The ballot credits eight names, and a three-person cap excludes Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose work on the New Keynesian Phillips curve, estimation and medium-scale models made the framework quantitatively usable. If the Committee judges that the estimation strand is part of the same achievement, no three-person set is clean, and this candidate then loses its main advantage over the others. A second concern is empirical. The post-2008 and 2021-23 inflation experiences leave the Phillips-curve slope and parameterisation open, so the citation must not imply forecasting success. A third is that earlier macro prizes on rational expectations, DSGE methods and time-series methods may be read as covering nearby ground. I think they covered methodology rather than the nominal-rigidity mechanism and policy-rule framework, but members who list this as a concern are not unreasonable. Finally, my own field is market and mechanism design, not macroeconomics. I rely on the common criteria and on colleagues' accounts of priority, and I cannot independently verify priority claims.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B014 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He separates originating a building block from refining or estimating it, and says the citation should credit the framework's conceptual and institutional role without claiming the baseline model forecasts well. He lists the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets estimation strand as a close alternative.
responses.response: I accept this distinction, and it is how I answer the chair's question. I would accept a citation confined to nominal-rigidity theory and policy rules, and I have narrowed my wording to that. I would defend the trio on stated criteria: each member has a distinct, citable originating contribution, and the three together cover mechanism, rule and synthesis. I would not call the estimation strand a footnote. If the Committee decides that the estimated medium-scale model is part of what it wants to honour, the three-person cap cannot hold that achievement together, and I would then favour a different candidate over a contested substitution. I do not think that is a reason to abandon the theoretical-originator reading, because the two strands are separable achievements.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B010 first for its clean two-person credit line. He is sceptical of B014 because of the eight credited names, the mixed evidence on the Phillips curve and the risk that earlier macro prizes cover nearby ground. His opening B014 trio was Woodford, Galí and Gertler.
responses.response: His attribution criterion is the right one, and it is the strongest argument against my own choice. B010 does have a cleaner credit line than B014. I still prefer B014 because the building blocks are more separable and have a much larger footprint in policy institutions. A trio of Woodford, Galí and Gertler credits the synthesis and application layer without the staggered-pricing and policy-rule ingredients it depends on, and I would not make that cut. On prior prizes, I read the rational-expectations and DSGE-methods awards as methodological, while this achievement concerns the nominal-rigidity mechanism and the rule framework. That is a judgement, and I accept he may weigh it differently. I keep B010 as my first alternative precisely because of its attribution cleanliness.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B032 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn, treating the China-shock design as a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution and Katz's skill-premium work as a distinct, earlier strand. She flags the task framework's credit outside the ballot and the debate over magnitude and persistence.
responses.response: I agree that Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the most identifiable unit on that ballot and that Dorn should be preferred to Katz for a trade-shock citation. I keep B032 as an alternative but not as my preferred part. The reasons are the one she names herself and one more. First, the conceptual half of the credit sits partly outside the ballot. Second, aggregate magnitude and persistence are still debated, and I do not know the latest re-examinations of shift-share inference well enough to call the designs settled. My criteria differ from hers only in weight. I give more weight to breadth and durability of a framework across decades of use, and she gives more to transparent identification. She should not read my ranking as dismissing her case.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first and keeps Calvo over Galí because Calvo's pricing device is the specific building block nearly every New Keynesian model uses. He treats the 2021-23 inflation as a test of empirical performance, not of the contribution, and he lists B010 and B042 as his alternatives.
responses.response: I agree on Calvo over Galí. In round 1 I said Galí deserves more weight than my own proposal gives him, and I still think that, but it is a reason to say so in the discussion, not a reason to drop the pricing device. I differ with Krusell slightly on how to treat the inflation episode. I would not call it irrelevant. It argues for the narrower citation I now propose, which names the rigidity mechanism and policy rules and makes no claim about the Phillips-curve slope or forecasting. I also note that he, Boppart and the chair are close co-authors, and that their agreement on this trio is not independent evidence. My view rests on the structure of the contributions.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first with Melitz and Helpman, accepts that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are an uncredited lineage, and says the citation should describe the selection and reallocation mechanism and avoid claiming a welfare magnitude. She holds the preference somewhat less firmly than in her opening.
responses.response: I think her wording discipline is right, and it is why I keep B010 as an alternative. A two-person Melitz-Helpman credit is easier to defend than my three-person B014 cut. I also see B010 as distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize, because it concerns heterogeneity across firms within industries. My remaining hesitation is the one she and Strömberg state: the size of selection-based welfare gains depends on functional form, and the uncredited lineage is real. If the Committee decides that attribution cleanliness should outweigh breadth of policy consequence, B010 is where I would move. I would not move to B016, because of partial overlap with the 2024 prize and observational identification in part of the evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants to honour the theoretical originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or the estimation and synthesis strand (Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets). A three-person cap cannot hold both, and this is the question most likely to move me to another candidate.

Whether Galí should replace or join Woodford. I regard Calvo and Taylor as the least substitutable names, and I would defend Woodford as the welfare-theoretic synthesis, but the choice between Woodford and Galí is closer than the other two.

How much weight the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation debates should carry. I treat them as shaping citation wording, not as undermining the originating contributions, but I cannot resolve the Phillips-curve evidence from the supplied material.

Whether the Committee reads earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, DSGE methods, time series) as covering this achievement. Prior-prize statements, including that Gertler was not a 2022 laureate, are members' and my own recollection and have not been independently verified here.

Whether B042 (Kiyotaki and Moore) should be elevated as a fallback, since eight members list it. I accept its two-person attribution is the cleanest on the list, but the collateral channel is better established as theory than by direct identification, and the 2022-prize overlap is unresolved. I have therefore kept B010 and B032 as my named alternatives.

What would move me: agreement that the estimation strand belongs in the same award, or a Committee preference for attribution cleanliness over breadth. In either case I would move to B010 first and B032 second, not to a different three-person B014 cut.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I find no connection in the supplied profile to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, or to the credited names on B010 and B032. My documented connections are SSE affiliation alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, and long-standing co-authorship in matching, auctions and market design. None involves a credited candidate here. I also note that my 2020 presentation speech was delivered for the Academy and does not establish a personal prize preference. My own field of market and mechanism design is not represented on this shortlist, so I do not see field proximity as a bias toward any candidate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
